problem: Complete graph $K_n$ can be expressed as the union of $k$ bipartite graphs if and only if $n \leq 2^ k$ (proof understanding as in D.B West)
proof_numbered:
0001 | I was going through the text "Introduction to Graph Theory" by Douglas West where I came across the following theorem.
0002 | 
0003 | >Theorem. The complete graph $K_n$ can be expressed as the union of $k$ bipartite graphs if and only if $n \leq 2^ k$ . 
0004 | >
0005 | >>Proof: We use induction on $k$. 
0006 | >>
0007 | >>Basis step: $k = 1$. Since $K_3$ has an odd cycle and $K_2$ does not, $K_n$ is itself a bipartite graph if and only if $n \leq 2$. 
0008 | >>
0009 | >>Induction step: $k > 1$. We prove each implication using the induction hypothesis. Suppose first that $K_n = G_1 \cup . . . \cup G_k$ , where each $G_i$ is bipartite. We partition the vertex set into two sets $X$, $Y$ such that $G_k$ has no edge within $X$ or within $Y$. The union of the other $k - 1$ bipartite subgraphs must cover the complete subgraphs induced by $X$ and by $Y$. Applying the induction hypothesis to each yields $|X| \leq 2^{k-1}$ and $|X| \leq 2^{k-1}$, so $n \leq 2^{k-l} + 2^{k-l} = 2^ k$ . 
0010 | >>
0011 | >>Conversely, suppose that $n \leq 2^ k$ . We partition the vertex set into subsets $X$, $Y$, each of size at most $2^{k-l}$. By the induction hypothesis, we can cover the complete subgraph induced by either subset with $k - 1$ bipartite subgraphs. The union of the $i$th such subgraph on $X$ with the $i$th such subgraph on $Y$ is a bipartite graph. Hence we obtain $k - 1$ bipartite graphs whose union consists of the complete subgraphs induced by $X$ and $Y$. The remaining edges are those of the biclique with bipartition $X$, $Y$. Letting this be the $k$th bipartite subgraph completes the construction. 
0012 | 
0013 | It's proof seem to be a bit difficult for me to understand in the first go, as here the author is talking about certain steps/constructions, which could have been better grasped if the material would have been provided with supporting figures. So this is my attempt of understanding the proof intuitively using figures.

0015 | First let us work out a simple example as follows:

0019 | On the left we have $K_4$. Now since $n=4=2^2$ we find it can be expressed as a union of two bipartite graphs as shown in the right (in red and cyan).

0021 | Now let us analyze each step of the proof.
0022 | 
0023 | >We use induction on $k$.
0024 | 
0025 | Here $k$ is the induction parameter 
0026 | 
0027 | >Basis step: $k = 1$. Since $K_3$ has an odd cycle and $K_2$ does not, $K_n$ is itself a bipartite graph if and only if $n \leq 2$. 
0028 | 
0029 | When $k=1$ it means that the complete graph $K_n$ can be expressed a union of only $1$ bipartite graph. Now this is possible only when the $K_n$ is itself a bipartite graph.
0030 | 
0031 | Now let us check for $n=4,3,2,1,..$
0032 | 
0033 | For $n\geq 3$ each of the $K_n$ shall have $C_3$ present in it, which being an odd cycle the graph as a whole shall not be bipartite.
0034 | 
0035 | For $n\leq 2$ this problem of having an odd cycle does not arise and as such the graph as a whole is a bipartite graph.
0036 | 
0037 | So we have proof for basis step as written in the text.
0038 | 
0039 | >Induction step: $k > 1$. We prove each implication using the induction hypothesis. Suppose first that $K_n = G_1 \cup . . . \cup G_k$ , where each $G_i$ is bipartite.
0040 | 
0041 | Our main aim should be such that for the current $k$ we can make use of the hypothesis assumed true for $k-1$.
0042 | 
0043 | >We partition the vertex set into two sets $X$, $Y$ such that $G_k$ has no edge within $X$ or within $Y$. The union of the other $k - 1$ bipartite subgraphs must cover the complete subgraphs induced by $X$ and by $Y$. Applying the induction hypothesis to each yields $|X| \leq 2^{k-1}$ and $|X| \leq 2^{k-1}$, so $n \leq 2^{k-l} + 2^{k-l} = 2^ k$ . 
0044 | 
0045 | We assume that our system is already having $k-1$ bipartite graphs ($G_1,G_2,...G_{k-1}$) and now we are working with the $k$th bipartite graph ( which is also present in the system). Now suppose that the $k$th bipartite graph is considered, only as far as its partite set is concerned. We are not considering its edges currently. 
0046 | 
0047 | Let $X$ and $Y$ be its two partite sets.
0048 | 
0049 | [![Fig 1][2]][2]
0050 | 
0051 | Now we are only left to add the edges from $X$ to $Y$ to make the entire graph a complete graph. Without the edges from $X$ to $Y$, each of $X$ and $Y$ are actually $K_{|X|}$ and $K_{|Y|}$.
0052 | 
0053 | Now without the $i$ th bipartite graph, we have $k-1$ bipartite graphs in this system, now using the induction hypothesis, (since $k-1<k$ , our hypothesis is true.) 
0054 | 
0055 | So for the $Y$ in cyan we have: $|Y|\leq 2^{k-1} \tag1$ 
0056 | 
0057 | Again for the $X$ in red we have: $|X|\leq 2^{k-1} \tag2$
0058 | 
0059 | Adding $(1) and (2)$ we have,
0060 |   
0061 | $$|Y|+|X|\leq 2.2^{k-1} \implies n \leq 2^{k}$$

0068 | >Conversely, suppose that $n \leq 2^ k$ . We partition the vertex set into subsets $X$, $Y$, each of size at most $2^{k-l}$. By the induction hypothesis, we can cover the complete subgraph induced by either subset with $k - 1$ bipartite subgraphs. The union of the $i$th such subgraph on $X$ with the $i$th such subgraph on $Y$ is a bipartite graph. Hence we obtain $k - 1$ bipartite graphs whose union consists of the complete subgraphs induced by $X$ and $Y$. The remaining edges are those of the biclique with bipartition $X$, $Y$. Letting this be the $k$th bipartite subgraph completes the construction. 
0069 | 
0070 | Now for the converse let us assume the $n\leq 2^k$. Now suppose we divide the entire set of vertices into two parts ($X$ and $Y$) such that each is having a size of at most $2^{k-1}$, (like $\frac{n}{2}\leq \frac{2^k}{2}$). We were initially having a complete graph on $n$ vertices. Due to the partition we have two complete subgraphs of size $|X|$ and $|Y|$. 
0071 | 
0072 | By the induction hypothesis, each of the the complete subgraphs $X$ or $Y$ has $k-1$ bipartite graphs.
0073 | 
0074 | Now if one does union of these two ($X$ and $Y$) it seems that we shall get $2^k$ bipartite graphs, but its not. Check the diagram below.
0075 | 
0076 | [![Fig][4]][4]  
0077 | 
0078 | On combining the $i$th bipartite graphs of each we can get only $2^{k-1}$ bipartite graphs on unions.
0079 | 
0080 | After this if we add the edges between $X$ and $Y$ we shall get the $k$ th bipartite graph.
